hook.line: Don Hernando drove a taxi for forty years, and he always had strong views on how a bus should take a hill. Spanish has one phrase for speeding up and another for going flat out.
hook.es: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
hook.en: The bus picked up speed on the way down.

examples.es: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
examples.en: The bus picked up speed on the way down.

examples.es: La moto iba a toda velocidad.
examples.en: The motorbike was going at full speed.
They left in a great hurry.

examples.es: Después del martes, la obra agarró velocidad.
examples.en: After Tuesday, the work picked up speed.

examples.es: El carro perdió velocidad en la subida.
examples.en: The car lost speed on the climb.

examples.es: Vale trabajó a toda máquina toda la noche.
examples.en: Vale worked flat out all night.

rule:
*Agarrar velocidad* is the process: something goes from slow to fast. It also works for plans and projects (*la obra agarró velocidad*). Its opposite is *perder velocidad*.

*A toda velocidad*, *a toda prisa* and *a toda máquina* describe the state: already going flat out. They come after the verb and say how.

In Latin America people say *agarrar* (also *tomar*) where Spain says *coger*. Avoid *coger* here.

The little words are fixed: *a toda*, never *en toda*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *a toda velocidad* an adverbial phrase of manner. *Agarrar velocidad* is a verb plus noun combination.

readAndPick.es: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
options: The bus lost speed downhill.
The bus picked up speed downhill.
The bus was going at full speed.

readAndPick.es: La moto iba a toda velocidad.
options: The motorbike picked up speed.
The motorbike slowed down.
The motorbike was going flat out.
They left in a great hurry.
They left slowly.
They left at the end.

readAndPick.es: Después del martes, la obra agarró velocidad.
options: The work stopped after Tuesday.
The work was fast on Tuesday.
The work sped up after Tuesday.

readAndPick.es: El carro perdió velocidad en la subida.
options: The car lost speed on the climb.
The car picked up speed on the climb.
The car went flat out on the climb.
Hernando picked up speed.
Hernando drove flat out.
Hernando slowed down.

readAndPick.es: Vale trabajó a toda máquina toda la noche.
options: Vale slowly started work all night.
Vale stopped work in the night.
Vale worked flat out all night.

readAndPick.es: El tren agarra velocidad poco a poco.
options: The train gradually picks up speed.
The train always goes at full speed.
The train gradually loses speed.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose and type: "The motorbike was going at full speed." La moto iba ___ velocidad. (a toda / en toda)
yourTurn.answer: La moto iba a toda velocidad.
yourTurn.why: The fixed phrase is *a toda velocidad*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose and type: "The bus picked up speed on the way down." El bus ___ en la bajada. (agarró velocidad / iba a toda velocidad)
yourTurn.answer: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
yourTurn.why: Picking up speed is a change, so use *agarró velocidad*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "They left in a great hurry."
yourTurn.why: *A toda prisa* tells how they left.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "The car picked up speed on the highway."
yourTurn.answer: El carro agarró velocidad en la autopista.
accept: El carro tomó velocidad en la autopista.
yourTurn.why: A change from slow to fast is *agarrar velocidad*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change it: *El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.* Now the bus loses speed on the climb (*la subida*).
yourTurn.answer: El bus perdió velocidad en la subida.
yourTurn.why: The opposite of *agarrar velocidad* is *perder velocidad*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "Hernando never used to drive at full speed."
yourTurn.answer: Hernando nunca manejaba a toda velocidad.
accept: Hernando nunca manejó a toda velocidad.
yourTurn.why: *A toda velocidad* comes after the verb and says how he drove.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: "Mariana left in a great hurry."
accept: Mariana se fue a toda prisa.
yourTurn.why: Same phrase, one person: *a toda prisa* after the verb.

pitfalls.wrong: El bus cogió velocidad en la bajada.
pitfalls.right: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
pitfalls.why: Almost. In Latin America *coger* is best avoided, so say *agarró* (or *tomó*).

pitfalls.wrong: La moto iba en toda velocidad.
pitfalls.right: La moto iba a toda velocidad.
pitfalls.why: The fixed phrase starts with *a*, not *en*.

pitfalls.wrong: El bus agarró a toda velocidad en la bajada.
pitfalls.right: El bus agarró velocidad en la bajada.
pitfalls.why: Keep them apart: *agarró velocidad* is the change, *a toda velocidad* is the state.

personal: Think of something in your life that picked up speed lately, and say it with *agarró velocidad*.
